families.t: risk assessment, policy, worker involvement, machinery, fire, dust, chemicals, manual handling and public protection
f: Textile employers and self-employed people are responsible for protecting workers and others affected by their activities.
Textile-sector guidance covers fire, dust, chemicals, dyes, knives, machinery, bale handling, noise and musculoskeletal risks.
A proportionate management system should include risk assessment, a health and safety policy and worker involvement.
Responsibilities extend to employees, part-time and casual workers, trainees, customers, neighbours, visitors and the public.
Textile machinery standards address mechanical, electrical, thermal, noise, ergonomic, fire and explosion hazards.
Machine selection and safeguarding should reflect the specific textile process and foreseeable access to danger zones.
Health risks and machinery risks should be managed together rather than as separate programmes.
Arrangements should be reviewed when processes, machinery, substances, staffing or workplace layout change.
families.g: Textile risk depends on process, machinery, fibres and chemicals, work organisation, maintenance, competence, exposure, fire precautions and people who may be affected.

families.s: HSE spinning-machinery guarding, isolation and safe-work guidance
families.t: drives, shafts, interlocks, brakes, cleaning, carriage access, emergency stops, doffing, loose clothing and competent adjustment
f: Drive parts and shafts on spinning machinery should be guarded or made safe by position.
Interlocks are expected where regular access to hazardous areas is required.
Rear areas of single-sided frames should be blocked off or fully guarded.
Brakes should work correctly and be inspected through a defect-reporting system.
Machines should be isolated before workers enter or work inside carriage areas.
Emergency stops should be accessible along older machines where existing safeguards require them.
Adjustment and minor repair access should be limited to trained people following documented safe systems.
Loose clothing, jewellery and unsecured hair should be prohibited around rotating and moving parts.
families.g: Spinning-machine risk depends on machine design, speed, guarding and interlocks, access, braking, isolation, cleaning and doffing methods, maintenance and operator competence.

families.s: HSE textile dyeing and high-temperature dyeing-machine safety guidance
families.t: hot surfaces, steam, vessels, overflow, drainage, pits, lone working, pressure, door interlocks and maintenance
f: Hot parts on dyeing machinery should be guarded or insulated.
Steam injection nozzles should use noise-reduced designs where practicable.
Controls on open vessels should be positioned to avoid exposure to overflowing or boiling liquor.
Pits and gullies should be guarded, fenced and clearly marked.
Separate liquor-preparation rooms need emergency-contact arrangements for lone workers.
High-temperature dyeing machines operating above 100°C require pressure and locking hazards to be controlled.
Door locking and safety devices should be maintained and not defeated or misused.
Safe procedures should cover operation, pressure release, opening, inspection, maintenance and defect response.
families.g: Dyeing-machine risk depends on temperature and pressure, liquor and chemicals, vessel and door design, steam, drainage, access, isolation, safety devices and maintenance.

families.s: HSE cloth-finishing and fabric-coating machinery safeguarding guidance
families.t: roller nips, drives, belts, shafts, braking, hot surfaces, hydro-extractors, stenters, cutting blades and corrosion
f: Drive points, belts and shafts on finishing and coating machinery should be correctly guarded.
Roller intakes should have suitable guards, interlocks or trip devices.
Braking systems should be checked regularly.
Hot parts and pipes should be guarded or insulated to prevent burns.
Hydro-extractors should have functioning interlocked lids and out-of-balance protection.
Stenter chain, sprocket and roller-nip hazards should be guarded.
Slitting and cropping blades should be guarded and sharpening restricted to appointed competent people.
Corrosive processing liquids can accelerate equipment deterioration, so inspection and maintenance should address corrosion.
families.g: Finishing and coating risk depends on roller and drive hazards, machine speed, heat, chemicals, corrosion, guarding and interlocks, braking, blade work, access and maintenance.

families.s: HSE fabric-cutting and industrial-sewing machine safety guidance
families.t: cutting tables, blade guards, warning signals, trip guards, chain-mail gloves, blade changing, needles, drive parts and housekeeping
f: Cutting-table danger areas should be marked and access restricted by barriers.
Motorised and automatic cutting tables should indicate when the blade is moving.
Automatic adjustable guards should cover the exposed part of a cutting blade.
Suitable five-finger chain-mail gloves should be available and worn for cutting and blade handling.
Blade-changing and disposal should follow a documented safe system.
Industrial sewing standards address needles, drives, programmable movement, electricity, noise, heat and ergonomics.
Sewing-machine guarding should prevent access to hazardous drive and needle mechanisms while allowing the intended task.
Cleaning should prevent accumulations of fluff, fly and off-cuts around machines and electrical equipment.
families.g: Cutting and sewing risk depends on blade and needle exposure, automatic movement, guards, table layout, operator hand position, PPE, blade changing, housekeeping and competence.
